docs.title: XL Marinade
docs.text:
Deterministic Excel formula-graph extraction to SQLite — with optional, bring-your-own-key LLM documentation.

Excel workbooks that drive real business decisions (actuarial models, pricing tools, finance workbooks) accumulate thousands of formulas across dozens of sheets, with no audit trail beyond "open it and trace the references by hand." XL Marinade parses a workbook once and writes its entire formula graph — every cell, every cross-sheet reference, every VBA-driven mutation — into a provenance-stamped SQLite database you can query, diff, and document like any other data asset.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
• Formula graph extraction — every formula cell becomes a node; every reference (same-sheet or cross-sheet) becomes an edge, so you can query "what feeds this cell" or "what does this cell feed" with SQL instead of Ctrl+[.
  • Cross-sheet dependency resolution — references across sheets and named ranges are resolved into the same graph, not left as opaque strings.
  • Canonical formula families — structurally identical formulas repeated down a column or across a block (the common "one row per asset/policy" pattern) are grouped into a single family with a deterministic ID, instead of being treated as thousands of unrelated formulas.
  • VBA edges — macro-driven mutations (e.g. paste-special / .Value = .Value overwrites) are captured as edges in the same graph, so a value that "changes by magic" via a macro is still traceable.
  • Provenance-stamped SQLite output — the output database carries a schema version and per-edge provenance, so downstream tooling can rely on it as a versioned contract rather than reverse-engineering table shapes.

docs.title: Deterministic core, LLM-optional
docs.text: extract, diff, and the baseline document output are 100% deterministic and network-free — the same workbook always produces the same graph, and nothing ever leaves your machine. An optional bring-your-own-key LLM tier layers narrative documentation and VBA enrichment on top, and degrades gracefully back to the deterministic output if no key is configured. See LLM add-on.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
uvpip

New to uv?

uv is a fast Python package and project manager. Install it once and the command above will work:

# macOS / Linux
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

# Windows (PowerShell)
powershell -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"

Prefer a Python you already have? pipx install uv (or pip install uv) works too. Full options are in the uv installation guide.

pip install xl-marinade

Requires Python 3.11+. uv tool install puts the marinade CLI on your PATH — run marinade --help from anywhere. To use XL Marinade as a library in your own project instead, uv add xl-marinade and run it with uv run marinade.

docs.title: Optional extras
docs.text:
XL Marinade's core (extract, diff, deterministic document), including VBA macro parsing, needs no optional dependencies. One add-on is opt-in:

uvpip 
# Optional LLM-enriched documentation (bring your own API key)
uv tool install 'xl-marinade[llm]'

# Optional LLM-enriched documentation (bring your own API key)
pip install 'xl-marinade[llm]'
  • [llm] — adds the bring-your-own-key LLM documentation tier (--enrich, xl_marinade.llm). See LLM add-on for setup and configuration.
  • [vba] — no longer needed, and kept empty so existing install commands keep working. Since 0.7.0 every install parses VBA macros: macro-driven mutations show up as edges in the formula graph and marinade diff reports macro changes (see VBA extraction). Before 0.7.0 this extra installed oletools.

The extra doesn't change the deterministic behavior of extract, diff, or plain document — they only add capability on top.

docs.title: LLM add-on
docs.text: extract, diff, and document are fully deterministic and never touch the network. The optional [llm] add-on layers LLM-generated narrative documentation (and an opt-in VBA enrichment pass) on top of that deterministic output, using a provider and key you supply. Enrichment is advisory only: if it's unavailable, misconfigured, or errors out, it always falls back to the same deterministic output you'd get without it — it never blocks or raises.

docs.title: 1. Install the extra
docs.text: pip install 'xl-marinade[llm]'

docs.title: 2. Set your API key
docs.text:
Either variable works; LLM_API_KEY takes precedence if both are set:

export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."

docs.title: 3. Enrich
docs.text:
Add --enrich on the CLI, or call the xl_marinade.llm entry point directly:

marinade document ir.db -o out/ --enrich       # LLM-written narrative documentation
marinade extract book.xlsx -o ir.db --enrich   # opt-in LLM VBA enrichment

from xl_marinade.llm import document

document("ir.db", "out/")   # uses the configured key

With the [llm] extra installed but no key configured, enrichment degrades to deterministic documentation — it never raises or blocks. Enrichment is the only network call in the tool, and your workbook data is sent only to the endpoint you configure.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
All configuration is via environment variables — the key is read at call time and never stored. Both enrichment paths (document --enrich and the opt-in extract --enrich VBA pass) go through the same client seam, so they honour the same variables:

Variable Purpose Default LLM_API_KEY / OPENAI_API_KEY API key (required to enrich) — OPENAI_MODEL Model name gpt-5.2 LLM_BASE_URL OpenAI-compatible endpoint override OpenAI's API LLM_PROVIDER Provider id, recorded in the audit log (openai, azure, openai_compatible) openai

VBA enrichment uses a cheaper default model

marinade extract --enrich honours the same variables above — including LLM_BASE_URL, so it stays on your configured endpoint. The one difference: when OPENAI_MODEL is unset it defaults to a cheaper model than document --enrich, because it makes one call per VBA procedure. Set OPENAI_MODEL to pin a specific model for both.

docs.title: Azure, local, or proxied models
docs.text:
The add-on speaks to any OpenAI-compatible endpoint via LLM_BASE_URL — Azure OpenAI, a local vLLM/Ollama server, or a LiteLLM proxy — for both document --enrich and extract --enrich:

export LLM_API_KEY="..."
export LLM_BASE_URL="http://localhost:11434/v1"   # e.g. a local Ollama server
export OPENAI_MODEL="llama3.1"
marinade document ir.db -o out/ --enrich

docs.title: Failure mode is always "fall back," never "break"
docs.text:
Enrichment sits strictly on top of the deterministic core:

  • No [llm] extra installed → --enrich degrades to deterministic documentation.
  • Extra installed, no key configured → same graceful degradation.
  • Key configured but the request errors (bad endpoint, rate limit, network failure) → same graceful degradation.

In every case you still get the deterministic documentation.md and model_spec.json that marinade document produces without --enrich — the LLM tier can only add to that output, never replace it with something worse or block the run.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: The core workflow is three commands: extract a workbook's formula graph, document it, and diff two versions of it. All three read and write local files; none of them make a network call unless you explicitly ask for LLM enrichment.

docs.title: 1. Extract
docs.text:
marinade extract book.xlsx -o ir.db

Parses book.xlsx and writes its entire formula graph — every formula cell, every cross-sheet reference, every canonical formula family — into the provenance-stamped SQLite database ir.db. -o/--out defaults to ir.db if omitted.

docs.title: 2. Document
docs.text:
marinade document ir.db -o out/

Reads the IR database and writes deterministic documentation into out/: documentation.md (human-readable) and model_spec.json (machine-readable). No network call is made.

To layer optional LLM-written narrative documentation on top (requires xl-marinade[llm] and an API key — see LLM add-on):

marinade document ir.db -o out/ --enrich

If the [llm] extra isn't installed, or no key is configured, --enrich degrades gracefully to the same deterministic output as step 2 — it never blocks or errors.

docs.title: 3. Diff
docs.text:
marinade diff a.db b.db

Compares two extracted databases (e.g. before/after a workbook revision) and emits a JSON changelist to stdout — every formula added, removed, or changed, by canonical family where applicable. Use -o/--out to write the changelist to a file instead of stdout.

docs.title: What's network-free vs. opt-in
docs.text:
Command Network calls marinade extract None, unless you pass --enrich (opt-in LLM VBA enrichment) marinade document None, unless you pass --enrich (opt-in LLM narrative documentation) marinade diff None — always deterministic

--enrich is the only opt-in network call anywhere in the tool. Everything else — extraction, diffing, and baseline documentation — is 100% deterministic and runs entirely on your machine.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Three end-to-end how-tos, each self-contained and copy-pasteable. Every workbook below is built inline with openpyxl — generic cell content, no client data — so you can run each example verbatim and get the exact output shown.

docs.title: Extract a workbook and query its dependencies
docs.text:
First, build a tiny synthetic workbook: a 5-period amortization with two formula columns that depend on each other — Balance this period depends on last period's Balance and Decay, and Decay this period depends on this period's Balance.

Save as make_book.py:

import openpyxl

wb = openpyxl.Workbook()
ws = wb.active
ws.title = "Sheet1"
ws["A1"] = "Month"
ws["B1"] = "Balance"
ws["C1"] = "Decay"
ws["A2"] = 0
ws["B2"] = 1000
ws["C2"] = 0
for row in range(3, 8):
    prev = row - 1
    ws[f"A{row}"] = row - 2
    ws[f"B{row}"] = f"=B{prev}-C{prev}"
    ws[f"C{row}"] = f"=B{row}*0.02"
wb.save("book.xlsx")

python make_book.py
marinade extract book.xlsx -o ir.db

Now query the binding-level dependency graph — agent_binding_dependencies — with the sqlite3 CLI:

sqlite3 -header -column ir.db \
  "SELECT from_label, to_label, kind, edge_count FROM agent_binding_dependencies
   ORDER BY from_label, to_label;"

from_label  to_label      kind     edge_count
----------  ------------  -------  ----------
Balance     Decay         formula  1
Balance     Sheet1!A1:C2  formula  1
Decay       Balance       formula  1

Three edges: Balance reads Decay and the seed row (A1:C2, the header + period-0 constants, which didn't get a label of its own), and Decay reads Balance right back — the cyclic binding graph described in Bindings & the graph. (The ORDER BY from_label, to_label gives a stable row order — edge rows are otherwise unordered.) Same query from Python:

import sqlite3

con = sqlite3.connect("ir.db")
con.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
rows = con.execute(
    """
    SELECT from_label, to_label, kind, edge_count
    FROM agent_binding_dependencies
    ORDER BY from_label, to_label
    """
).fetchall()
for row in rows:
    print(dict(row))

{'from_label': 'Balance', 'to_label': 'Decay', 'kind': 'formula', 'edge_count': 1}
{'from_label': 'Balance', 'to_label': 'Sheet1!A1:C2', 'kind': 'formula', 'edge_count': 1}
{'from_label': 'Decay', 'to_label': 'Balance', 'kind': 'formula', 'edge_count': 1}

docs.title: Diff two versions of a model
docs.text:
Build two versions of the same tiny model — v2 changes the Decay formula's multiplier from 0.02 to 0.03, nothing else:

Save as make_versions.py:

import openpyxl


def build(decay_rate: float) -> openpyxl.Workbook:
    wb = openpyxl.Workbook()
    ws = wb.active
    ws.title = "Sheet1"
    ws["A1"] = "Month"
    ws["B1"] = "Balance"
    ws["C1"] = "Decay"
    ws["A2"] = 0
    ws["B2"] = 1000
    ws["C2"] = 0
    for row in range(3, 8):
        prev = row - 1
        ws[f"A{row}"] = row - 2
        ws[f"B{row}"] = f"=B{prev}-C{prev}"
        ws[f"C{row}"] = f"=B{row}*{decay_rate}"
    return wb


build(0.02).save("model_v1.xlsx")
build(0.03).save("model_v2.xlsx")

python make_versions.py
marinade extract model_v1.xlsx -o a.db
marinade extract model_v2.xlsx -o b.db
marinade diff a.db b.db -o changelist.json

The changelist (see Diffing workbooks for the full field reference) reports the change once, at the binding level, not once per cell:

{
  "summary": {
    "total_changes": 7,
    "bindings_formula_changed": 1,
    "cells_formula_changed": 5,
    "ir_inference_changes": 0
  },
  "changes": [
    {
      "seq": 2,
      "type": "BINDING_FORMULA_CHANGED",
      "sheet": "Sheet1",
      "address": "C3:C7",
      "old_formula": "RC[-1]*0.02",
      "new_formula": "RC[-1]*0.03",
      "layer": "workbook",
      "modification_kind": "logic_change"
    }
  ]
}

bindings_formula_changed: 1 is the number that matters for review — the five cells_formula_changed entries are the same edit, once per cell in the Decay column, rolled up into that one BINDING_FORMULA_CHANGED entry. modification_kind: "logic_change" (rather than reference_shift) confirms this is a real formula edit, not just references moving because of an insertion elsewhere in the sheet. ir_inference_changes: 0 says nothing in the extractor's inference layer moved. When something does — a table candidate, a binding's label evidence, or a lookup's edges re-resolved because its key changed value — those entries carry "layer": "ir_inference": consequences of an edit, not edits. Every change carries a layer, so keep the workbook layer before you review a changelist:

import json
from pathlib import Path

changelist = json.loads(Path("changelist.json").read_text())

workbook_edits = [c for c in changelist["changes"] if c["layer"] == "workbook"]
for change in workbook_edits:
    if change["type"] == "BINDING_FORMULA_CHANGED":
        print(
            f"{change['address']}: {change['old_formula']} -> "
            f"{change['new_formula']} ({change['modification_kind']})"
        )

C3:C7: RC[-1]*0.02 -> RC[-1]*0.03 (logic_change)

docs.title: Generate documentation (deterministic, then enriched)
docs.text:
Using the ir.db from the first example:

marinade document ir.db -o out/

Writes out/documentation.md (human-readable) and out/model_spec.json (machine-readable) — no network call is made. Both describe the same two calculated variables from the extraction above (Balance, Decay), their inferred role (Calculation), and which of them need reconciliation against a reference implementation.

To layer LLM-written narrative documentation on top, install the extra, set a key, and pass --enrich (see LLM add-on for provider setup):

pip install 'xl-marinade[llm]'
export OPENAI_API_KEY="sk-..."
marinade document ir.db -o out/ --enrich

--enrich degrades gracefully rather than failing: without the [llm] extra installed, marinade document ... --enrich prints note: xl-marinade[llm] not installed — deterministic documentation only and writes the exact same deterministic documentation.md/model_spec.json as the plain command above. The same fallback applies if the extra is installed but no key is configured, or the request errors — you always get the deterministic output, and enrichment can only add to it, never replace it with something worse or block the run.

docs.title: Bindings & the graph
docs.text:
A binding is a labelled group of cells that represents one variable in the model — a whole column ("Policies In Force", one value per projection month), a single input cell ("Discount Rate"), or a block of assumptions. Extraction groups the raw cell-level graph into bindings so that auditing a model means reasoning about its variables, not walking thousands of individual cell references one at a time.

A binding is always a contiguous rectangular range on a single sheet, and it is one of two kinds:

  • formula — the cells share a repeated formula pattern (e.g. the same formula, position-adjusted, down every row of a column).
  • constant — the cells hold input values with no formula.

docs.title: A tiny worked example
docs.text:
Take a two-column projection sheet, one row per month:

Cell Formula Meaning B2 =B1-C1 Policies in force this month = last month's in-force − last month's lapses B3 =B2-C2 (same pattern, next row) ⋮ ⋮ ⋮ C2 =B2*0.02 Lapses this month = 2% of this month's in-force C3 =B3*0.02 (same pattern, next row) ⋮ ⋮ ⋮

Column B collapses into one binding — call it pols_if — and column C collapses into another, pols_lapse. Instead of a graph with one node per cell, you now have a graph with two nodes: a variable, not a spreadsheet coordinate.

docs.title: How bindings relate: binding edges
docs.text:
Bindings are connected by edges derived from the underlying cell references: if any cell in one binding refers to any cell in another, an edge connects the two bindings (with a count of how many underlying cell references it represents). Extraction also recognizes VBA-driven dependencies the same way — a macro that paste-as-values a template row into an output block produces a binding edge too, tagged with the procedure responsible; see VBA extraction.

Binding graphs can be cyclic. In the example above, pols_if this month depends on pols_lapse last month, and pols_lapse this month depends on pols_if this month — cell by cell, that's a strict DAG (nothing depends on its own future), but collapsed to bindings, pols_if and pols_lapse depend on each other. This is normal for any recursive projection model, not a defect: extraction handles cyclic binding graphs correctly and always produces a stable ordering over them, so tooling built on top (documentation, lineage walks) doesn't need to special-case recursive models.

docs.title: Why bindings are the useful audit unit
docs.text: A model with 10,000 policy rows and 50 calculated columns has 500,000 formula cells but on the order of 50 model variables. Auditing at the cell level means drowning in near-duplicate edges; auditing at the binding level means answering the question an actuary or analyst actually asks — "what does Net Cashflow depend on, and what depends on it?" — with a handful of named variables instead of a wall of cell coordinates.

docs.title: Recalculating with marinade calc (experimental)
docs.text:
Experimental

marinade calc and marinade values are experimental. They sit outside the SemVer contract that covers the SQLite output: file formats, status names and refusal rules can change in any release. Do not build a pipeline that cannot absorb that.

An extracted workbook stores results only for the inputs sitting in it, often a single policy. marinade calc answers a different question: given other input values, what do the output cells become? It recalculates the workbook with IronCalc, proves itself against the workbook's own stored values first, and puts a status on every value it returns. marinade values returns the stored values in the same row shape, without recalculating.

The rule behind the design: a missing value costs a missing comparison, a wrong value with an "ok" label costs a wrong conclusion. When the calculator cannot vouch for a value, it refuses it and says why.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install 'xl-marinade[calc]'

marinade values works on the base install. marinade calc needs the extra (it pins ironcalc==0.9.1); without it the command exits with code 5.

docs.title: The files in
docs.text:
Option File What it holds WORKBOOK .xlsx / .xlsm The model, saved by Excel so it carries stored values. --policies policies.csv One row per input set. An id column plus one column per mapped field. UTF-8 (save from Excel as "CSV UTF-8"). Values are read exactly as written, spaces included; ids stay text and lose surrounding spaces, also where the id is mapped to a cell. A blank value (empty or only spaces), a duplicate id, a duplicate column name or a row with more values than the header has names (an unquoted 250,000) is an error, and so is a value under a column with no name. Columns with no name (the empty trailing columns some exports add) are ignored while they are empty, and so are empty values past the last column. --map map.json Which cell or defined name each field sets. --outputs repeatable Output cells, ranges or defined names ('Results!B5:B64'). Ranges expand to cells. --variables vars.json Optional. Named output variables for rows.csv. --check-against check.json Optional. Stored results for other input sets, to widen the trust run.

You must give at least one of --outputs and --variables. A key repeated in the same object of map.json, vars.json or check.json is an error: JSON would keep only the last one.

docs.title: Targets
docs.text:
Every cell entry (map.json fields, --outputs, vars.json, and the output and selector entries of check.json) takes a cell (Inputs!C3), a range (Proj!C11:C130) or a defined name. The sheet entries of check.json take a sheet name, in any case. Sheet names and defined names ignore case letter by letter, as in Excel (Straße and Strasse stay two names), and names may use letters of any script (Ärger, 税率). A file that defines two names differing only in case, which Excel itself does not allow, has a target naming them refused as ambiguous.

A name can be defined for the whole workbook or for one sheet only (a sheet copied in from another workbook often brings its own). Write a sheet's own name as 'Sheet'!Name. A bare name means the workbook's definition; when a sheet defines the same name too, a bare name is refused as ambiguous, and the error says how to write each.

A whole column or row (Calc!B:B, Calc!3:3, or a name over one) covers the part of it the sheet uses: up to the last row (or column) that holds a cell. A target that covers no cells is an error that names it: a name that holds a formula (OFFSET(...) dynamic ranges included), a constant, a broken reference (#REF!) or cells in another workbook, and a whole column or row outside the range the sheet uses. Give such a target as a plain range instead. When several targets are wrong, the error names each of them.

A name whose reference is relative (written without $ on its row or column, such as Calc!B5 or Calc!$B5) names different cells from each cell that uses it, so it is refused as a target too.

Inside formulas, names are read the way Excel reads them: a formula reads its own sheet's definition of a name first, and the workbook's only when the sheet has none.

docs.title: map.json
docs.text:
{
  "id_field": "policy",
  "fields": {"age": "Inputs!C3", "term": "Inputs!C4", "rate": "Rate"}
}

id_field names the policies column that holds the id (default id). It may also appear in fields, so the id is written into a workbook cell as well. Each target must be a cell or defined name that holds a constant; mapping onto a formula is an error, and so is mapping onto any cell of an array formula's range (Excel cannot hold a constant there). The same holds for a check.json selector. Mapping two fields onto one cell (by address, by name, or one of each), the id field included, is an error too, since the cell can hold only one of their values.

A field that no formula can read is an error too: its value would change nothing, and every policy would get the stored inputs' answer as ok (a map one cell off, on the label beside the input, is the usual cause). A field counts as read when any formula's cell or range reference covers its cell, an empty one included, or when a formula reads it through a defined name in any form Excel resolves (Name, a sheet's own name, 'Sheet'!Name), through a name holding a formula, or inside CELL, INFO or GETPIVOTDATA. A field is refused only when no read can reach it: where a read cannot be placed (an OFFSET or INDIRECT landing beyond the cell it lands on with the stored inputs, a name holding OFFSET or INDIRECT, a name with a relative reference, a 3-D reference such as S1:S3!B1), every cell it may reach is accepted. A Sheet!Name that no definition answers is #NAME? in Excel, so it reads nothing. The id field is never refused, since it may be written into a display cell. A field read only by outputs you did not request is accepted. run.json records, under inputs, the cell each field sets and whether a requested output reads it.

Before each input set, every mapped input is reset to its stored value. A value outside the cell's data-validation list refuses that input set's outputs.

Values are converted the way Excel converts what is typed into the cell, by the type of the value the cell holds:

  • A number cell takes a plain decimal (40, -1.5, .5, 4e1, 0042) or an ISO date (2024-06-30), which becomes its Excel serial (45473). Spaces around it are ignored, as Excel ignores them when it enters a number; other white space, such as the non-breaking space pasted text often carries, is refused by name.
  • A boolean cell takes TRUE or FALSE, in any case.
  • A text cell takes the text as written, spaces included (" A " is four characters), even when it looks like a number, less one leading apostrophe: Excel's entry prefix, so '123 sets the text 123.
  • A cell the workbook saved empty takes an ISO date as its serial, TRUE/FALSE (any case) as a boolean and a plain decimal as a number; any other text stays text.

On a number cell or an empty one, these are errors that name the policy, the field and what is wrong, rather than a guess:

  • spellings Excel reads by the locale's rules: 5%, 1,000, 1,5, 1.234.567, $100, (100), 4 000, digits other than 0-9 (٤٠, １２３), fractions (1 1/2), times and date-times (12:30, 3:2, 2024-06-30T12:00), and dates not written YYYY-MM-DD. Give a plain decimal or an ISO date instead;
  • a leading apostrophe ('123): Excel makes the rest text, which a number or empty cell would not hold as calc reads it, so give the value without it;
  • error values such as #N/A;
  • numbers outside the range Excel accepts (1e-400, 1e400);
  • ISO dates before 1900-03-01. Excel's 1900 date system counts a 29 February 1900 that never was, so its serials before March 1900 are a day off the calendar, and it has no dates before 1900. Give the serial number instead.

A date not written YYYY-MM-DD is text some locale reads as a date: digits joined by /, - or . whose parts can be a day (1-31), a month (1-12) and a year (one or two digits, or four from 1900), in day-month-year, month-day-year or year-month-day order (30/06/2024, 6/30/2024, 30.06.2024, 2024/06/30), or two of them (10-20, 6/2024, 2024-06); or an English month name, in any case, with a day or year (30-Jun-2024, June 30, 2024, Jun 2024). Other text stays text on an empty cell, so ids and codes such as 123-45-6789, 1234-5678 or 100-200 written into a blank display cell are kept as written.

A number cell also refuses any other text (1_000, abc, inf, nan); on an empty cell those stay text, as in Excel. --check-against table values are set with the type they are stored with: a table cell holding TRUE sets a boolean.

A number keeps every digit it is written with. Excel keeps 15 significant digits of a number typed into a cell and turns the rest to zeros (1234567890123456789 becomes 1234567890123450000), so a policy value with more than 15 significant digits (a long policy number used as a lookup key, or a value written by a script with 17 digits) can compute differently from Excel typing it. Values set by a macro or a query keep full precision in Excel too.

The list is the validation's literal items, or the stored values of its source: a range, a whole column (the cells it holds) or a defined name over cells (the validation sheet's own name first, as in a formula). As in Excel, the check compares the value as it is entered in its cell. Items typed into the validation itself ("01,02") are text as written: they match ignoring case, or by value when the entry is a number. Items read from cells keep the cells' types: text ignores case, and a number matches number items only, so 2025-01-01 typed into a date cell matches a list of cells holding that date, while 1 typed into a number cell does not match a cell holding the text 001. What is not checked:

  • A list fed by a formula (INDIRECT, OFFSET, a name holding one, as in cascading dropdowns) or by a table column (Table1[Code], or a name over one) is not checked in this version: any value is accepted there.
  • A list held in formula cells is read from the values the workbook stored, not recomputed for the input set.
  • Only list validations are checked. Whole-number, decimal, date, length and custom validations are not.

docs.title: vars.json
docs.text:
{
  "premium": {"range": "Proj!C11:C130", "period_start": 0},
  "reserve": {"range": "Proj!H11:H130", "period_start": 1},
  "npv":     {"cell": "Summary!B4"}
}

A range runs down one column or across one row of one sheet; a 2-D range, or a name whose areas lie on more than one sheet, is an error. A name with several areas on one sheet runs in row order, whatever order its areas were written in. period_start is required on every range and has no default, because workbooks differ on whether periods count from 0 or 1. Periods count from it: the first cell of the range is period period_start, the next one period_start + 1. A single cell has no period (the column is empty) and must not carry period_start.

docs.title: check.json
docs.text:
Optional. It names results the workbook already holds for other input sets, such as a batch-results sheet, so the trust run can recalculate those input sets too and compare.

{
  "results": {"sheet": "Results", "id_column": "A", "first_row": 2,
              "outputs": {"Summary!B13": "C"}},
  "inputs": {"table": {"sheet": "Inputs", "id_column": "A", "first_row": 2,
                       "fields": {"age": "B", "term": "C"}}}
}

results.outputs maps an output cell to the results-sheet column holding its stored value per input set; two outputs that resolve to one cell are an error. inputs has exactly one of table (a column per map.json field) or selector (a single cell, e.g. "Control!C4", that picks the input set by id; it may be a mapped field's cell too). Only input sets the engine reproduced count towards the exercised paths.

A mismatch (an input set whose recalculated output differs from the stored one by more than --tolerance) refuses that output only for policies that took the same path to it:

  • For the mismatching set, the run records its path to the output: the outcome of every branch and lookup-edge probe upstream of the output.
  • A policy whose own outcomes for those probes are all the same gets check_against_mismatch on that output, and the output is refused.
  • If any of those probes is unplaced, or its reading is unsure (for the set or for the policy), the paths count as the same and the output is refused. The rule errs toward refusing.
  • An output with no branch or lookup probes upstream has only one path, so a mismatch on it refuses it for every policy.
  • A policy on a different path is judged by the usual rules: ok if a matching input set (or the stored inputs) checked its path, unverified_path if nothing did.

trust_report.json lists every mismatch under check_against.mismatches: the input set id (input_set), the output (cell), stored, computed, and relative_difference (measured the way the tolerance is: relative, or absolute below 1).

docs.title: When you need --check-against
docs.text: When a workbook stores results for only one input set, give --check-against whenever it holds results for others (a batch-results sheet, a scenario table). Without it, the trust run sees only the paths the stored inputs take. A lookup that lands in the middle of a table for a new policy (a different age row, a different year) and a branch the stored inputs do not take stay unverified, so most new values come back unverified_path. Measured on lifelib BasicTerm (10,000 model points stored in Batch_Results, selector Control!C4): with no check set, 100% of new values came back unverified_path; with 200 checked points, 100% came back ok, and all of them were correct.

docs.title: How a run works
docs.text:
1. Read the workbook's calculation settings. 1904 dates, precision as displayed or a Strict Open XML file refuse the whole workbook (exit code 6).
  2. Extract the formula graph into a temporary database, or reuse --ir if it matches the workbook. Give --ir a database extracted with 0.8.1 or later: earlier ones trimmed formulas' text results and dropped "" results, which the trust run then fails. An older one is refused (exit code 1) with "re-extract with marinade extract". The version checked is the one the extracting install stamped into the database.
  3. Scan the formulas for refused patterns.
  4. Load a copy with every formula's stored value deleted, so the engine has to compute. The trust run compares each formula cell with what Excel stored, within --tolerance (default 1e-9, relative or absolute), on the stored inputs and on every --check-against input set.
  5. Add probe cells on a hidden sheet that report which branch, lookup row, rounding input and dynamic reference each input set reaches. Probes go only into cells upstream of the requested outputs and into the cells a dynamic reference among them can land on (see Statuses), and never into a cell that is already refused. A probe is the part of the cell's formula it reports on, lifted onto that sheet so it computes what the cell computes: references keep their sheet (quoted where Excel needs it, as for '2024'), operators keep Excel's precedence (A&B="x" is (A&B)="x"), and under --as-of TODAY() and NOW() read the as-of date, as the cells do.
  6. For each policy: reset, set the inputs, recalculate, read outputs and probes.
  7. Walk the graph from each output back to its roots and assign a status.

The extraction database is never written by calc. The run clears its own known output files from -o at the start (results.csv, rows.csv, paths.csv, trust_report.json, run.json), so a failed run cannot leave stale ones behind. Nothing else in the directory is touched. Before clearing anything, the run refuses (exit code 1) an -o that is a file rather than a directory, and an input file that is one of those output files (the same name in -o, or the same file through a link): clearing it would delete your input.

The probe cells go on a hidden sheet named _marinade_probes. A workbook that already has a sheet of that name (in any case) is refused when the run needs probes; rename the sheet in a copy of the workbook.

docs.title: The files out
docs.text:
All in the -o directory, UTF-8, \n line endings, no timestamps.

File Contents results.csv policy_id, output (Sheet!A1), value, status, reasons. One row per policy and output cell. rows.csv With --variables: policy, variable, period, value, status, reasons. paths.csv policy_id, cell, family, kind, ordinal, outcome, exercised. The branch or lookup edge each policy took, in the cells that fed its outputs: through the cells its dynamic references landed on for that policy, not the cell an OFFSET starts from or where it landed with the stored inputs; ordinal tells apart several probes of one kind in one cell; exercised is true when the trust run took it too. trust_report.json formula_cells, checked, reproduced, share, failures, refused_patterns, settings (with settings.refused), held_external_links, check_against (input_sets, and mismatches with input_set, cell, detail, stored, computed, relative_difference), probes_unplaced (probes that could not be placed, for any reason) and probes_over_cap (those left out only because --probe-cap was reached). run.json ironcalc_version, marinade_version, workbook_sha256, tolerance, as_of, probe_cap, probes_unplaced, per variable its range, period_start and the cell period 0 falls on, and per map field (inputs) the cell it sets (target) and whether a requested output reads it (read_by_requested_outputs: true, false, or "unknown" when only a read that cannot be placed, as above, may reach it).

marinade values writes rows.csv and run.json (variables only). Its rows carry status stored, and the policy is stored, or the stored value of the id field (id_field, default id) when --map maps it, written as policies.csv would hold it (555, TRUE), so its rows join calc's rows for the same input set.

In reasons, each entry reads kind@root:detail, joined by ;, in a stable order. The root is the cell the problem starts at; it can be upstream of the output.

docs.title: Statuses
docs.text:
Every output gets a value. A value can carry several reasons; its status is the most serious.

Status Meaning refused The output depends, through the graph, on a cell that failed the trust run or matches a refused pattern, or a --check-against input set on the same path did not reproduce it. The value is returned for inspection but must not be used. The reason names the root cell. uncertain The value rests on something implementation-dependent: a rounding function whose input sits within about 1e-12 relative of the point where the result flips, or a comparison or sorted lookup whose two sides are that close (but not equal). A rounding or comparison probe that could not be placed also lands here (not_checked_value). unverified_path The policy took a branch or lookup position the trust run never exercised, so those formulas were never checked against Excel. A branch or lookup probe that could not be placed also lands here (not_checked_path). ok None of the above. stored marinade values only: the workbook's own stored value.

Details worth knowing:

  • Exact whole-number inputs to INT, TRUNC, ROUNDUP, ROUNDDOWN, CEILING and FLOOR are not uncertain (nothing can flip). Exact halves into ROUND and MROUND are.
  • A comparison whose two sides are exactly equal is decided, not near: IF(t=0, ...) with t exactly 0 stays ok. Only sides that differ by more than nothing and at most about 1e-12 relative are near_comparison. The same holds for an approximate lookup whose value equals its matched key.
  • Branches are IF, IFS, SWITCH, CHOOSE, IFERROR and IFNA, and an XLOOKUP with an if_not_found argument (outcomes found and not_found; the argument counts only when nothing was found). A branch counts as exercised if any cell in the same canonical formula family took it in the trust run. Lookups (VLOOKUP, HLOOKUP, MATCH, LOOKUP, XLOOKUP and XMATCH, in every match and search mode calc accepts) count per family too, but the table's first row, last row and "beyond the end" must each have been hit. For XLOOKUP and XMATCH first and last are positions in the lookup array, whichever way the search runs.
  • Only evidence that was checked counts. A cell that failed the trust run, or is a refused pattern, exercises nothing for its family. A branch or lookup inside an arm the formula did not evaluate (the FALSE arm of an IF that went TRUE) is not exercised by the trust run and is not a path a policy took. A --check-against input set exercises only the branches and lookups upstream of the outputs it was compared on, following its own dynamic references: the cells an OFFSET or INDIRECT landed on for that set count, the cell an OFFSET starts from and the cell it lands on with the stored inputs do not (unless the set landed there).
  • Because probes are placed only upstream of the requested outputs, asking for fewer outputs can make a status more conservative: a family member that is not upstream of any requested output is not probed, so it cannot vouch for the branches it took. This holds while every probe fits under --probe-cap; past it, more outputs means more probes competing for the cap, and a status can become more conservative with more outputs too.
  • A probe that cannot be placed (cap hit, or inside LET/LAMBDA/an array context) never yields ok: a branch or lookup probe gives unverified_path, a rounding or comparison probe uncertain, and a dynamic-reference or number-to-text probe refused.
  • OFFSET and INDIRECT are followed to where they point for each input set; if that cannot be read, the outputs behind it are refused (dynamic reference not checked). So is a range whose end is a call, such as SUM(C5:OFFSET(C5,Term-1,0)) or B1:INDIRECT(...): it covers the smallest rectangle holding both ends, read per input set; one whose ends lie on two sheets is refused (Excel gives #VALUE! there). IronCalc 0.9.1 answers #VALUE! for a range ending in INDEX (A1:INDEX(...)) and #ERROR! for one whose start names its sheet (Proj!C5:OFFSET(...)), so the trust run refuses those. The cells that decide where a reference points (OFFSET's rows, columns, height and width, the cells INDIRECT's text is built from) are precedents of the cell, so a failure or an untried branch there reaches it. An OFFSET whose base is a sheet's own (sheet-scoped) name is always refused this way, and a branch, lookup, rounding or comparison on such a name is never ok: the probe sheet cannot read the name as the formula's sheet does. Such an OFFSET brings no sheet into the landing region below, and a name with a relative reference counts as no fixed cells among the cells that decide where a reference points.
  • The cells a dynamic reference lands on are checked like cells upstream of an output. Every formula cell on the sheet an OFFSET starts from (or a built range lies on), or that an INDIRECT text names literally ("Rates!B"&row), is probed, with everything upstream of it, so the trust run and --check-against input sets exercise their branches and lookups and a policy landing on an untried arm is unverified_path. These probes count toward --probe-cap after those of the requested outputs. An INDIRECT whose text names no sheet ("A"&row, or a sheet name read from a cell) can land anywhere, so its landing cells are not probed: each formula cell it lands on that no probe covers, and each such cell upstream of it, gives not_checked_path (reached through a dynamic reference, not probed), plus what its own probes give when they cannot be placed (not_checked_value for a rounding or comparison, refused for a dynamic reference or number-to-text). A landing on a constant needs no check. An INDIRECT text that addresses a cell off the grid (row 0, below row 1,048,576 or right of column XFD) counts as unread: Excel gives #REF! there, while IronCalc 0.9.1 reads Rates!B0 as 0.
  • An error code Excel does not have (IronCalc's #N/IMPL!, #ERROR!, #CIRC! and the like) in an output or in a probe is an engine_error for that policy, so the output is refused, even when an IFERROR around it would have turned it into a plausible value. Excel's own error codes (#N/A, #DIV/0!, #VALUE! and the rest) are values like any other, with one exception: a #NAME? in an output for a policy, where the trust run had none in that cell, is an engine_error. Excel's #NAME? comes from the formula's text, not its inputs, so one only a new policy reaches is a function the engine lacks on an arm the trust run never took.
  • Every cell of an array formula's range is a formula cell, whether a legacy (Ctrl+Shift+Enter) array or a dynamic array that spills. Excel stores the formula on the range's top-left cell only; calc reads the other cells as computed by it. Each is compared in the trust run (and counted in formula_cells), and each carries the formula's status: a refusal, failure or probe that could not be placed (every probe inside an array formula) reaches it and every cell reading it. When a policy makes a dynamic array spill past the range the workbook stored (SEQUENCE(n) with a larger n), the cells it spills into carry the formula's status too.
  • A passing trust run proves only the paths the stored inputs take. That is what unverified_path and --check-against are for.

docs.title: Reason kinds
docs.text:
silently_wrong (engine value differs from Excel's, no error), engine_error, macro_function, unsupported_function, no_stored_value, refused_pattern, check_against_mismatch and input_outside_allowed_values give refused. near_rounding_flip, near_comparison and not_checked_value give uncertain. unexercised_branch, unexercised_lookup_edge and not_checked_path give unverified_path. external_link_held is informational and leaves the status ok.

A #NAME? from the engine is macro_function when the cell, or any cell upstream of it, calls a VBA function (the engine cannot run VBA); the root is that UDF cell, the smallest one if several feed it. It is unsupported_function only when no UDF is involved: the engine does not know a function the cell uses.

docs.title: What ok means, and what it does not
docs.text: ok means every formula and every path behind the value was checked against values Excel stored: on the stored inputs, or on a --check-against input set that took the same branches and lookup edges. It does not guarantee that a new input set's value is within --tolerance of what Excel would compute for it. Floating-point differences between the engine and Excel are tiny, but cancellation can amplify them: a net figure that is a small difference of large present values can move by more than 1e-9 relative even when every formula reproduced. On lifelib BasicTerm_SE one model point's net cash-flow present value came out at 1.003e-9 relative to Excel's, against the default tolerance of 1e-9. Choose --tolerance for the outputs you compare, and treat agreement with Excel beyond it as likely, not proven.

docs.title: Memory and output size
docs.text:
results.csv, paths.csv and rows.csv are written one policy at a time, flushed as each policy finishes, so memory does not grow with the number of policies. Nor does it grow with the number of --check-against input sets: each matching set's branch and lookup outcomes are folded into the exercised set as it finishes and its readings dropped; a mismatching set keeps only its path to the output it missed. Peak memory is set by the workbook (the formula graph, the engine's copy of the workbook and the probe plan) and by the output cells you request: a range is expanded cell by cell, so Calc!B1:B1048576 costs memory for a million cells. A whole column (Calc!B:B) expands only over the rows the sheet uses.

The files on disk do grow with the policies. paths.csv has one row per policy per branch or lookup probe it reached, which for an actuarial projection can be over a thousand rows per policy: about 1.2 million rows and 126 MB for 1,000 lifelib BasicTerm_S policies. An OFFSET that sums over a projection adds more, since every row it covers fed the output. Leave room in -o for it.

docs.title: --probe-cap
docs.text:
--probe-cap (default 50,000) bounds the probe cells a run places. A probe left out because the cap was reached never yields ok (see Statuses), so a run that hits the cap is more conservative, not wrong. When it happens, probes_over_cap in trust_report.json counts the probes left out, and marinade calc prints one line on stderr with the cap that would place them all:

warning: 73006 probes did not fit under --probe-cap 50000, so the values behind them
are not ok; rerun with --probe-cap 123006 to place them all

OFFSET projections use the cap fastest. Every formula cell on the sheet an OFFSET starts from is probed, with everything upstream of it, so a projection of 3,000 rows by 40 columns needs well over 50,000 probes. Those landing-region probes are planned after the probes of the requested outputs' own cells, in sheet, row and column order, so the end of the projection is the first to go past the cap: policies landing late in the term come back uncertain or unverified_path with not checked reasons. Raise the cap to the number the warning gives; a larger cap costs memory and run time roughly in proportion, and paths.csv grows with the probes each policy reaches.

A run that stops part-way (a bad value in policies.csv, for instance) deletes results.csv, paths.csv and rows.csv, so partial results never look complete.

docs.title: Refused patterns
docs.text:
Some formulas reproduce Excel on the stored inputs only by luck and silently disagree on the next. They are refused even when the trust run reproduces them. The detail is:

Detail What triggers it approximate lookup on unsorted column VLOOKUP/HLOOKUP/MATCH/LOOKUP in approximate mode over keys that are not sorted, or that are text outside plain a-z, 0-9 and space (Excel's collation differs from a plain sort). Also XLOOKUP/XMATCH with a binary-search mode, or a search mode the scan cannot read. approximate lookup on mixed text and numbers The key column mixes types. approximate lookup on a non-range table The table is not a plain reference. approximate lookup on whole column The table is a whole column or row, or a name over one. IronCalc counts empty cells; Excel skips them. implicit intersection on multi-cell name A single-cell use of a defined name that covers several cells (a name over a whole column or row always does). implicit intersection on multi-cell range A multi-cell range used outside a function argument. Ranges inside SUMPRODUCT, MMULT and similar are fine. name holds a formula A formula reads a defined name whose definition is a formula or a constant rather than cells (the detail text says "formula" for both). IronCalc 0.9.1 rejects such names. name with a relative reference: <Name> A formula reads a defined name whose reference is relative (no $ on its row or column). Excel reads it relative to the cell using it; IronCalc 0.9.1 reads the stored reference as it is. Also put on a mapped input whose dropdown list is such a name, which refuses everything that input feeds. RAND, RANDBETWEEN, RANDARRAY Always. TODAY, NOW Unless --as-of YYYY-MM-DD is given; then they are replaced by that date. circular reference Always (iterative calculation is noted in the report, not honoured). data table What-If data tables are removed before loading and their cells refused. unparseable formula The formula could not be parsed. Error literals typed into a formula, such as #N/A, are a known source of these. external reference not held The formula reads an external reference the engine copy cannot hold: a range, one with no cached value (IronCalc returns #ERROR! or #REF! for those), or a defined name that points into another workbook. approximate lookup on input-dependent keys An approximate lookup whose key cells change with a mapped input (an input cell, or a formula that depends on one). The keys may be sorted for the stored inputs and not for the next policy. function IronCalc does not implement: NAME The formula calls a function the installed IronCalc cannot compute. calc asks the engine about every function the workbook calls, so this covers Excel functions IronCalc 0.9.1 does not have (AGGREGATE, BAHTTEXT, CALL, the CUBE… functions, DBCS, DETECTLANGUAGE, EUROCONVERT, FIELDVALUE, FILTERXML, GETPIVOTDATA, GROUPBY, IMAGE, JIS, PHONETIC, PIVOTBY, REGISTER.ID, RTD, SQL.REQUEST, STOCKHISTORY, TRANSLATE, WEBSERVICE), ones it knows but has not implemented (the FORECAST.ETS family), functions newer than the engine, and VBA and add-in functions (also when Excel lacks them too). The engine answers #NAME? or #N/IMPL!, error values an IFERROR, ISERROR or ISNUMBER around the call would turn into a plausible value. LET and LAMBDA parameters called like functions are not affected; a LAMBDA held in a defined name gets every check in this table through its body, for every cell that calls it. Calls the engine computes only for some arguments are refused by shape: SHEETS with a reference for SHEETS(ref); RANK over a single cell or RANK over a computed reference (also RANK.EQ, RANK.AVG) unless the list is written as a range; NAME over a range for DATEDIF, DATEVALUE, FORMULATEXT, N and UNICODE given a range, a LET or LAMBDA parameter, or an expression over one (a range inside a function that returns one value does not count: SUM, COUNT and the like, INDEX with literal non-zero row and column, or a lookup of one value). Excel computes these cell by cell in an array formula or SUMPRODUCT; the engine answers one #N/IMPL!.

Some refusals are per policy, read from the probes:

Detail What triggers it lookup value type differs from keys An approximate lookup matches a key of a different type than its lookup value (text against numbers). Excel finds nothing there (#N/A); IronCalc 0.9.1 returns a row. number-to-text at a decimal tie TEXT, FIXED or DOLLAR rounds a number that sits within about 1e-12 of a tie at the format's decimals: TEXT(1234.5,"#,##0"), TEXT(0.0125,"0.0%"), FIXED(1.005,2). Excel rounds the tie away from zero on the 15-digit value (1,235); IronCalc 0.9.1 rounds the binary value and can land on the other side (1,234). At an exact binary tie FIXED and DOLLAR happen to agree with Excel; they are refused all the same. number-to-text of a negative value that rounds to zero or one unit TEXT with a one-section format shows a negative number that rounds to zero or to one unit of its last place: TEXT(-0.01,"0%"), TEXT(-1,"0"), TEXT(-0.4,"0"). Excel keeps the minus sign (-1%, -1, -0); IronCalc 0.9.1 drops it. A format with a negative section (0;(0)), FIXED and DOLLAR are not affected. number-to-text where Excel's 15-digit text differs A number becomes text through &, CONCAT, CONCATENATE, TEXTJOIN or a text function (LEN, LEFT, MID, SUBSTITUTE, EXACT, FIND, VALUETOTEXT, the REGEX functions, TEXTSPLIT and the like), and its text needs more than 15 significant digits (7/12, 0.1+0.2) or the number lies outside 0.0001 to 1e15, where Excel may write scientific notation. Excel writes at most 15 significant digits; IronCalc up to 17. Also TEXT, FIXED or DOLLAR showing more than 15 digits. criterion built with & from a non-integer number A SUMIF, SUMIFS, COUNTIF, COUNTIFS, AVERAGEIF, AVERAGEIFS, MAXIFS or MINIFS criterion such as "<="&x where x is not a whole number. Excel compares against the 15-digit text it wrote.

Integers, and decimals with up to 15 significant digits that sit on no tie, stay ok. TEXT with a date or time format needs no check, and a format's third section (shown only for an exact zero) does not decide the rounding. A range joined by TEXTJOIN, CONCAT or CONCATENATE is read cell by cell: constants that are text, booleans, blanks or numbers Excel writes as the engine does need nothing; formula cells (every cell of an array formula's range among them, and the empty cells below or right of a dynamic array that its spill can grow into), mapped inputs and other numbers are read per policy. Each such cell is probed once, however many joins read it, and these probes are planned after every other probe, so they never take --probe-cap room from a branch or lookup check; a join whose cells did not fit under the cap is refused as number-to-text not checked for its own cell and what depends on it, nothing else. A function result joined as text (XLOOKUP, INDEX, IF) is read like a number when it is one value; when it is an array, or the join names a range with more than 1,000 cells to read, or a sheet's own name or a name with a relative reference, the join is refused as number-to-text not checked for the policies that evaluate it, not for those whose branch skips it.

A conversion calc cannot check at all is refused for every policy as number-to-text not checked, whatever the policy: a TEXT format that is not literal text, or that calc cannot read (General, @, scientific, fractions, conditions, first two sections that round differently); a range given to a text function such as LEN; or a conversion inside an array formula, LET/LAMBDA, or beyond --probe-cap.

docs.title: Diffing workbooks
docs.text:
marinade diff compares two extracted IR databases — the SQLite output of marinade extract — not two raw workbook files directly. Extract each version of the workbook first, then diff the two databases:

marinade extract before.xlsx -o a.db
marinade extract after.xlsx  -o b.db
marinade diff a.db b.db

This is deterministic and network-free: the same pair of databases always produces the same changelist.

docs.title: Why compare databases, not files
docs.text: Comparing raw formula text between two workbook versions is noisy: inserting a row shifts every absolute reference below it, so a plain text diff reports hundreds of "changes" for a single row insertion. marinade diff first matches sheets and rows/columns between the two versions and re-expresses version A's addresses in version B's coordinate space, so a row insertion is reported once — as a row insertion — instead of as a formula change on every cell it shifted.

docs.title: The changelist
docs.text:
The output is a JSON object with these top-level keys:

Key Contents version The changelist format version (currently "1.0"), not a workbook version. schema_version_a / schema_version_b The IR schema version each input database was extracted with. workbook_sha256_a / workbook_sha256_b The provenance hash of each source workbook, carried over from extraction. root_a / root_b The extraction root (sheet + range), if either database was a rooted extraction; null for a full-workbook extraction. summary Counts of changes by category — bindings added/removed/moved/resized/formula-changed, cell value/format/dtype changes, sheet and row/column edits, VBA modules and procedures, and more (see below). binding_map A flat list mapping every binding in A to its match in B (or null if added/removed), each with a diff_state of unchanged, modified, moved, removed, or added, and shifted (true when only an inserted or deleted row/column changed its address). changes The ordered list of individual changes that make up the diff.

Each entry in changes is {"seq": <position>, "type": <change type>, ...}, where the remaining fields depend on the change type (e.g. a formula change carries old_formula and new_formula; a resize carries old and new shapes).

docs.title: Workbook edits vs. IR inference
docs.text:
Not every entry in changes represents something a person edited in the workbook. Some of extraction's output is inferred — table-candidate detection, binding-label evidence, binding metadata, and time-axis annotations are all derived by the extractor's semantic layer, and can shift between two extractions even when the cells they name were not touched. Every entry carries a "layer": "workbook" for an edit, "ir_inference" for inference. The inference layer is rolled up separately in summary.ir_inference_changes, so a consumer that only cares about actual workbook edits can filter it out rather than mistaking it for a genuine change.

Edge changes are classified per change. An edge that appeared or disappeared because its cell's formula changed is part of that edit ("workbook"). An edge out of a cell whose formula is unchanged is "ir_inference": nothing edited that formula, so the extractor re-resolved it against something else that did change. The common case is a lookup — INDEX/MATCH or VLOOKUP resolved to the row its key currently selects — whose key changed value. The key's own VALUE_CHANGED is the edit; the lookup's moved edges are its consequence.

docs.title: VBA changes
docs.text:
For a macro-enabled workbook, the diff also compares the VBA recorded in vba_modules and vba_procedures. These entries are workbook edits ("layer": "workbook") and come after every other change:

Type Meaning VBA_MODULE_ADDED / VBA_MODULE_REMOVED A module (module, e.g. BatchRunner.bas) exists in only one version. Its procedures are also reported as added/removed. VBA_PROCEDURE_ADDED / VBA_PROCEDURE_REMOVED A procedure exists in only one version. A removal with "ambiguous_rename": true had several equally likely rename targets, each reported as added. VBA_PROCEDURE_LOGIC_CHANGED The body changed beyond comments, whitespace and case. VBA_PROCEDURE_SIGNATURE_CHANGED As above, and the declaration line changed (signature_a / signature_b). VBA_PROCEDURE_RENAMED / VBA_PROCEDURE_RENAMED_AND_MODIFIED The same procedure under a new name in the same module (procedure_a → procedure_b), with or without a body edit. VBA_PROCEDURE_COSMETIC_CHANGED Only comments, whitespace, case or line continuations changed. VBA_DECLARATIONS_CHANGED Module code outside every procedure changed: Option statements, Declares, module-level variables and constants. VBA_DECLARATIONS_COSMETIC_CHANGED Only comments, whitespace or Attribute lines outside procedures changed.

Procedure entries carry module, procedure, kind, compile_branch and the line range (lines, or lines_a / lines_b for a matched pair; 1-based and inclusive) to look the bodies up in vba_procedures. Two branches of an #If block that define the same procedure are compared branch to branch. summary counts them as vba_modules_added, vba_modules_removed, vba_procedures_added, vba_procedures_removed, vba_procedures_renamed, vba_procedures_logic_changed, vba_declarations_changed and vba_cosmetic_changes.

Each database records whether its VBA was read in ir_metadata key vba_extraction (see VBA extraction). Trust the VBA_* entries only when both sides are extracted or no_vba_project. A database extracted by 0.5.0–0.6.x without the [vba] extra (skipped_no_oletools) has no VBA, so diffing it against one that does reports every module as added or removed: re-extract it first. When the key differs between the two databases, the changelist also carries an IR_METADATA_CHANGED entry for it.

docs.title: Inserted and deleted rows and columns
docs.text:
Rows and columns are aligned per sheet before anything else is compared, so an insertion or deletion is reported once, where it happened, rather than as edits to everything after it:

  • ROWS_INSERTED / ROWS_DELETED / COLS_INSERTED / COLS_DELETED carry sheet, at_row or at_col (in B's coordinates for an insertion, A's for a deletion) and count, the number of contiguous occupied rows or columns in that block. summary.rows_inserted, rows_deleted, cols_inserted and cols_deleted count rows and columns, not events.
  • A binding that lay entirely in deleted rows or columns is reported as BINDING_REMOVED with "with_axis_deletion": true, and appears in binding_map as removed.
  • A binding that only shifted because of the edit is unchanged in binding_map, with "shifted": true. Its address_a and address_b differ by the shift; the axis event explains it. Every binding_map row carries shifted, so filtering on diff_state still yields only what was edited, and filtering on shifted lists what the edit pushed along. A binding that moved on its own is moved, not shifted.
  • Formulas are compared as Excel rewrites them: a relative reference that spans the inserted or deleted rows or columns is adjusted before comparison, and so are defined names whose range shifted. What remains is the edit's real consequences, such as a formula that read a deleted column and now holds #REF!.

Alignment uses each row's or column's full contents first. Where that leaves a stretch unmatched, it retries with reference offsets ignored, then with only the header labels and constants. A row or column whose contents and label both changed can still be paired with whatever sits at the same position inside the unmatched stretch.

docs.title: Reference shift vs. logic change
docs.text:
A formula change (BINDING_FORMULA_CHANGED) carries a modification_kind of either:

  • reference_shift — only the absolute row/column targets moved (typically because rows or columns were inserted elsewhere in the sheet); the underlying logic is identical.
  • logic_change — the formula's actual logic changed.

This distinction matters for review: a wall of reference_shift entries after a row insertion is expected noise, while a logic_change on a binding you didn't touch is worth a second look.

docs.title: Quoting-insensitive formula comparison
docs.text: Excel sometimes stores the same cross-sheet reference with or without single-quotes around the sheet name ('Sheet1'!A1 vs Sheet1!A1) depending on how the workbook was last saved, even though nothing about the reference changed. The diff normalizes this away before comparing formulas, so re-saving a workbook in a different Excel build doesn't manufacture spurious formula-changed entries.

docs.title: How extraction works
docs.text:
marinade extract turns a workbook into a queryable database in four conceptual stages. Nothing here requires opening Excel, and nothing leaves your machine.

workbook (.xlsx/.xlsm)
    │
    ▼
cells + formulas          — every cell, every formula, in both A1 and R1C1 form
    │
    ▼
the formula graph         — every reference becomes an edge (same-sheet, cross-sheet,
    │                        external, or range)
    ▼
bindings                  — cells collapsed into labelled model variables
    │
    ▼
SQLite (ir.db)            — provenance-stamped, versioned, queryable

docs.title: The formula IS the data
docs.text:
Extraction doesn't summarize or interpret the workbook — it records it. Every formula cell keeps its own formula text (both the A1 form you'd see in Excel and a position-invariant R1C1 form used to recognize repeated patterns), its value, its format, and its position. Nothing is computed or approximated; the database is a faithful, literal transcription of what the workbook contains. If you can see a formula in Excel, you can find that same formula, verbatim, in the output database.

Repetition is recognized rather than duplicated: a formula that repeats, structurally identical, down a column or across a block (the common "one row per policy/asset" pattern) is grouped into a single canonical family with a deterministic ID, instead of being stored as thousands of unrelated formulas.

docs.title: The formula graph
docs.text: Every reference a formula makes to another cell becomes an edge: same-sheet references, cross-sheet references, references to external workbooks, and range references (SUM(A1:A100)) are all resolved into the same graph rather than left as opaque strings. Macro-driven mutations (paste-special, .Value = .Value overwrites) are captured as edges too, so a value that "changes by magic" via a macro is still traceable — see VBA extraction.

docs.title: Bindings
docs.text: Individual cell-level edges are precise but not how anyone thinks about a model — a 10,000-row projection has as many cell nodes as it has rows. Extraction groups cells into bindings: labelled rectangular ranges that correspond to a single model variable (a whole column, a single input cell, a block of assumptions). Reasoning about a model then means reasoning about its variables, not its individual cells. See Bindings & the graph for what a binding is and how bindings relate to each other.

docs.title: Determinism
docs.text: The same workbook always produces the same graph — the same bindings, the same binding IDs, the same edges. Sheets and cells are processed in a fixed sort order, and every hash (cell structure, binding identity) is computed from sorted inputs, so extraction has no run-to-run variation to reconcile away. The output database also carries its own provenance: a schema version and a SHA-256 hash of the source workbook are stamped into the database itself, so two databases can be compared knowing exactly what schema and what workbook produced each one — this is what makes marinade diff possible (see Diffing workbooks).

docs.title: Network-free
docs.text: extract never makes a network call by default — parsing a workbook, building the formula graph, and writing the database are all local, offline operations. The only opt-in exception is --enrich, which layers an LLM-assisted pass on top for VBA references that static analysis can't resolve; see LLM add-on.

docs.title: Querying the result
docs.text: The output database is meant to be queried, not just archived. A stable set of agent_* views sits on top of the underlying tables and is the intended surface for that querying — the raw tables underneath are an implementation detail that can change between schema versions, while the views are the durable contract. The full set of views and their columns is covered in the schema reference.

docs.title: VBA extraction
docs.text:
VBA macros are parsed by every install of XL Marinade: a plain pip install xl-marinade reads them. Parsing is static -- nothing executes the macro. The VBA project (xl/vbaProject.bin in an .xlsm) is read with olefile, and its module source is decoded by XL Marinade itself, following Microsoft's published MS-OVBA format.

Before 0.7.0 this needed the [vba] extra, which installed oletools. That extra still exists, empty, so existing install commands keep working.

Every database records whether its VBA was read, in ir_metadata:

SELECT value FROM ir_metadata WHERE key = 'vba_extraction';
Value Meaning extracted The VBA tables hold the workbook's VBA. no_vba_project The workbook has no VBA project, e.g. any .xlsx. failed The VBA project could not be read, or storing it raised (see the extraction log). The tables may be empty or partial. skipped_no_oletools Only in databases extracted by 0.5.0–0.6.x without the [vba] extra: the workbook has a VBA project that was not read. Re-extract with 0.7.0 or later.

Empty VBA tables mean "no macros" only when the value is no_vba_project. The extraction progress line says the same: VBA: none (no_vba_project) for a workbook without macros, VBA: <n> procs, … (extracted) when it was read. Databases from before this key existed have no row for it.

docs.title: What gets captured
docs.text:
For every VBA project embedded in the workbook, extraction captures:

  • Modules — standard, class, form, and document modules, each with its full source text and a SHA-256 hash of that source.
  • Procedures — every Sub, Function, and property accessor, with its signature, parameters, body, and a hash of its normalized body (so two procedures that are byte-different but logically identical can be recognized as such). Event handlers (e.g. Worksheet_Change) are flagged as such, and conditionally-compiled twins (the #If Win64 ... #Else ... pattern used for 32-bit/64-bit API calls) are both kept rather than one overwriting the other.
  • The call graph — which procedures call which others, including calls made indirectly through the object model (reading or writing a property).
  • Cell references — which ranges, named ranges, and tables each procedure reads from or writes to.
  • Security findings — a keyword scan of the project, stored on each module in vba_modules.security_findings_json as {"type", "keyword", "description"} entries. AutoExec marks procedures Office runs on its own (Workbook_Open, Auto_Open, Document_Open, …). Suspicious marks calls that reach outside the workbook: running programs (Shell, WScript.Shell, PowerShell), network access (XMLHTTP, URLDownloadToFile), writing or deleting files, DLL Declares, the registry, CreateObject/GetObject, environment variables, keystrokes sent to other programs (SendKeys), Excel 4 macros, calls by computed name (CallByName), and reading or editing the VBA project itself. A finding flags code to review; it is not a verdict. A model that only reads and writes its own cells has none.

These become nodes and edges in the same graph that cells and bindings live in (see Bindings & the graph), so a procedure that writes to a range shows up as a dependency of that range, right alongside the formulas that also feed it.

docs.title: Deterministic paste provenance
docs.text:
A common macro pattern in cashflow and pricing workbooks copies a "template" row of formulas into an output block, one row per iteration, as a paste-as-values operation (PasteSpecial Paste:=xlPasteValues, or the equivalent .Value = .Value assignment). The destination cells end up holding constants, not formulas — so the formula graph alone can't trace from the output block back to the template row it was copied from; that lineage only exists in the macro.

Extraction recovers it: static analysis of the VBA source recognizes these paste patterns and synthesizes a bridging edge from the output block back to the template row it was copied from, tagged with the name of the procedure responsible. The result is fully deterministic and requires no execution or network access — the same macro source always produces the same bridging edges — so a value that "changes by magic" via a macro stays traceable to the specific procedure that wrote it.

docs.title: Comparing versions
docs.text: marinade diff compares the VBA of two databases module by module and procedure by procedure, including code outside procedures. It reports added, removed, renamed and edited procedures, and separates comment-only edits from logic changes. See VBA changes for the change types. Check vba_extraction on both databases first: a side extracted by an older version without the [vba] extra (skipped_no_oletools) makes every module look added or removed.

docs.title: Where LLM enrichment fits
docs.text: Static analysis can't resolve every reference — a range built up from string concatenation or computed at runtime, for example. The optional --enrich flag layers an LLM-assisted pass on top to infer those dynamic references. It's strictly additive to the deterministic VBA extraction above, requires the separate [llm] extra and an API key, and never runs unless you explicitly ask for it. See LLM add-on.

docs.title: marinade calc
docs.text:
Experimental. Recalculate a workbook for each policy in a CSV and report how far to trust each value. Needs xl-marinade[calc]. See Recalculating for the file formats, statuses and refused patterns.

marinade calc [OPTIONS] WORKBOOK

Argument

Name Description WORKBOOK Excel workbook (.xlsx/.xlsm). Required.

Options

Flag Description Default --policies FILE Policies CSV, one row per input set. Required. --map FILE map.json: field to cell or name, plus id_field. Required. --outputs TEXT Output cell, range or name ('Sheet'!Name for a sheet's own name); repeat for several. --variables FILE vars.json: named variables for rows.csv; period_start required on every range. --check-against FILE check.json: stored results for other input sets, to widen the trust run. --ir FILE Reuse this IR database (must match the workbook and be extracted with 0.8.1 or later). extract afresh --as-of TEXT Valuation date YYYY-MM-DD; replaces TODAY/NOW. unset (those cells are refused) --tolerance FLOAT Numeric comparison tolerance, relative or absolute. 1e-09 --probe-cap INT Maximum number of probe cells. When probes do not fit, a warning on stderr gives the cap that holds them all. 50000 -o, --out PATH Output directory. Required.

At least one of --outputs and --variables is required. Writes results.csv, rows.csv (with --variables), paths.csv, trust_report.json and run.json, after clearing those names from --out; an input file that is one of them is refused first.

Exit codes

Code Meaning 0 Success. 1 Error (bad input, unknown sheet, IR from another workbook or older than 0.8.1, an input that is one of the output files, an -o that is a file, the engine crashing on a formula). 5 xl-marinade[calc] is not installed. 6 The workbook is refused outright (1904 dates, precision as displayed, Strict Open XML).

Example

marinade calc model.xlsx --policies policies.csv --map map.json \
    --outputs 'Summary!B4' --as-of 2026-01-01 -o out/

docs.title: marinade values
docs.text:
Experimental. Write the workbook's stored values as variable/period rows, with status stored, in the same shape calc writes. No recalculation; works on the base install.

marinade values [OPTIONS] WORKBOOK

Options

Flag Description Default --variables FILE vars.json. Required. --map FILE map.json; its id field's stored value becomes the policy id. policy is stored --ir FILE Reuse this IR database (must match the workbook and be extracted with 0.8.1 or later). extract afresh -o, --out PATH Output directory (rows.csv + run.json). Required.

Exit codes

Code Meaning 0 Success. 1 Error (bad input, unknown sheet, IR from another workbook or older than 0.8.1, an input that is one of the output files, an -o that is a file).

Example

marinade values model.xlsx --variables vars.json -o stored/
